cues.text: Chapter five turns to emerging technologies and their contribution.
In earlier material we looked at what digital transformation is.
Now we ask a practical question: which technologies actually drive it, what does each one contribute, and what must we watch out for when we use it?
The source organises this as a table with three columns.
The first column is Technology.
The second is Contribution, meaning what the technology adds to an organisation.
The third is Example and caveat, meaning a typical use, together with a warning about what can go wrong or what must be checked.
Let us walk through it row by row, in order.
Row one: Cloud.
The contribution is elastic compute and shared services.
Compute simply means processing power.
Elastic means it can stretch and shrink with demand, so an organisation does not have to buy enough machines for its busiest day and leave them idle for the rest of the year.
Shared services means that common building blocks, such as storage, databases and software platforms, are provided by a provider and used by many customers.
The example is scaling registration traffic.
Think of a university opening online course registration: thousands of students log in during the first hours, then traffic falls away.
Cloud lets the system expand for the rush and contract afterwards.
The caveat is to monitor variable costs.
Because you pay according to use, the bill moves up and down, and if nobody watches it, a busy period or a badly configured service can produce unexpected charges.
Row two: AI/ML, that is artificial intelligence and machine learning.
The contribution is that these systems learn patterns, predict and classify.
Rather than following only rules a person wrote in advance, a machine learning system studies past data, finds patterns, and then predicts what is likely to happen or sorts new cases into categories.
The example is fraud detection.
A system learns what normal transactions look like and flags those that look suspicious.
The caveat is to validate accuracy and fairness.
Accuracy asks whether the system is right often enough to be useful.
Fairness asks whether it treats different groups of people in a balanced way, rather than wrongly flagging some customers more than others.
Both must be tested, not assumed.
Row three: Big data analytics.
The contribution is to analyse complex data at scale.
Big data refers to data that is large, varied and arriving quickly, and analytics is the discipline of examining it to find useful insight.
The example is forecasting demand, for instance estimating how much of a product customers will want so that stock and staffing can be planned.
The caveat is to protect privacy.
Large data sets often contain personal information, so organisations must safeguard it and handle it responsibly.
Row four: IoT, the Internet of Things.
The contribution is that connected sensors measure physical conditions.
A sensor is a small device that detects something in the real world, such as temperature, vibration or location, and connecting it to a network lets that reading flow into digital systems.
The example is monitoring machines, so that a factory can see the condition of its equipment.
The caveat is to secure devices.
Each connected device is a possible entry point for attackers, so it needs protection.
Row five: Blockchain.
The contribution is a shared tamper-evident history.
Think of a record book held jointly by many parties, where every entry is added to the history and any attempt to alter an earlier entry becomes visible.
Tamper-evident does not mean impossible to alter; it means changes can be detected.
The example is tracing goods, following a product through its journey.
The caveat is to verify inputs.
The record can show that something was written and has not been changed, but it cannot by itself prove that what was originally entered was true.
Someone must check the information going in.
Row six: Mobile and 5G.
The contribution is connectivity and convenient access.
Mobile devices put services in people's hands, and 5G, the fifth generation of mobile networks, supports faster and more capable connections.
The example is mobile service delivery, meaning that services such as payments, information or applications reach people through their phones.
The caveat is that coverage matters.
A service designed for mobile access is only useful where the network actually reaches, so areas with weak or no signal can be left behind.
Row seven: Automation, and within it RPA, robotic process automation.
The contribution is to execute repeatable tasks.
RPA uses software tools that carry out routine, rule-based steps that a person would otherwise perform by hand.
The example is reconciling invoices, which means matching invoices against related records to check that they agree.
The caveat is to handle exceptions.
Automation works well on the standard case, but unusual cases that do not fit the rules need a defined path, usually a person who can review and decide.
That completes the table.
Notice the pattern: every technology brings a real benefit, and every one carries a condition for using it well.
Costs must be watched, accuracy and fairness validated, privacy protected, devices secured, inputs verified, coverage considered, and exceptions handled.
Now let us step back and consider the longer view.
The source says that long-term impacts include new business models, increased reach, operational efficiency, data-driven strategy and innovation.
New business models means organisations can earn value in new ways.
Increased reach means they can serve more people and places.
Operational efficiency means doing work with less effort, time or waste.
Data-driven strategy means decisions guided by evidence from data.
And innovation means the continuing creation of new products, services and methods.
The source is equally clear that there are negative effects.

These may include job redesign, where roles change and people may need new skills; digital exclusion, where some people cannot access or use digital services; security threats; dependence on vendors, where an organisation relies heavily on outside suppliers; change fatigue,
where people become worn out by constant change; and environmental cost, since digital systems consume resources and energy.
So how should leaders respond?
The source says that managing transformation requires training, accessibility, fallback channels, governance and realistic funding.
Training prepares people to work with new tools.
Accessibility ensures that services can be used by as many people as possible.
Fallback channels give people another route, such as a counter or phone line, when the digital one fails or does not suit them.
Governance sets the rules, responsibilities and oversight for how technology is chosen and used.
And realistic funding means budgeting honestly for the full cost, not only the purchase.
The lesson of this chapter is balance: these technologies can contribute greatly to transformation, but only when their benefits are pursued together with their cautions.
